headline: weak
texts: Several core objectives need rebuilding, and that is useful information, not a verdict. Obstruction rewards a few anchors: the level of the block, strangulation signs, and the rule that resuscitation comes first. Start with the review cards flagged below, in the order shown, and redo the module after a day.

You are giving one most-common-cause for every setting. Redo the PYQ-versus-current-practice card, then say it aloud: PYQs expected hernia in India, adhesions lead wherever abdominal surgery is common, carcinoma leads in large bowel.

Causes are sitting in your head as an unsorted list. Rebuild it with three boxes: intraluminal (impaction, gallstone, bezoar), intramural (tumour, stricture, atresia, intussusception), extramural (adhesions, hernia, volvulus, external compression).

The timeline of features is not yet logical for you. Ask how much bowel lies beyond the block. High block: vomiting early, distension minimal, constipation late. Large bowel block: constipation and distension early, vomiting late. Redo the features card.

You are missing strangulation cues. Constant severe pain, tachycardia, fever, localised guarding and raised lactate mean ischaemic bowel, not simple obstruction. Reread the strangulation card and look for the changed pain word in every vignette.

Plain-film bowel identification needs rebuilding. Sketch both: central loops with folds that cross the lumen are small bowel; peripheral loops with partial folds are large bowel. Then attach 3, 6 and 9 cm to small bowel, colon and caecum.

You are stopping at the first test or the therapeutic one. Write the ladder: plain film first, contrast CT for level, cause and strangulation, ultrasound for a child with intussusception. Barium by mouth is unsafe in perforation or large bowel obstruction.
The signs are mixed together in your memory. Make a four-column card: sign, disease, test, one-line cue. Coffee bean, bird's beak, claw, target and Rigler's triad each get one row.

The management sequence is out of order for you. Redo it as a flowchart: resuscitate, check for strangulation, hernia or closed loop, then trial, then the 24-hour contrast check and the 72-hour limit. The old dictum is quoted but current practice differs.

Hernia risk and eponyms need a rebuild. Risk follows the neck, not frequency: femoral strangulates most. Then a three-line card: Richter equals partial wall, Littre equals Meckel's, Maydl equals W-shaped loop.

Child and adult intussusception are blurred. Child: usually idiopathic and ileocolic, enema reduction unless peritonitis, perforation, shock or failed reduction. Adult: pathological lead point, so resect. Redo that contrast card.

Site and bowel state are not yet driving your treatment choice. Sigmoid and viable: detorse and later colectomy. Gangrene or caecum: resect. Right colon cancer: right hemicolectomy. Left: Hartmann's. The caecum perforates first because it is widest.

These answers need a quick card. Gallstone ileus: enterolithotomy, stone usually impacted in terminal ileum. Ogilvie's: neostigmine, with atropine ready. Paralytic ileus: hypokalaemia is the commonest metabolic cause, treated with drip and suck.

You gave one most-common cause for every setting, so the old exam key and today's answer collided. Rehearse the pair: PYQs expected hernia in India; current practice says adhesions. Redo the PYQ-versus-current card.

You defaulted to adhesions and skipped the line saying no previous surgery. Adhesions need an operated abdomen. In a virgin abdomen, examine every hernial orifice first. Revisit the operated-versus-virgin card.

You treated intussusception as one disease with one enema cure. Children are mostly idiopathic; adults usually have a pathological lead point, often a tumour. Redo the child-versus-adult contrast and say 'adult: look for tumour, resect'.

You treated surgery as the safest default for a child with intussusception. A resuscitated, stable child without peritonitis gets image-guided reduction first. Learn the four surgical triggers: peritonitis, perforation, shock, failed enema.

You treated the first or therapeutic test as the definitive one. Plain film shows the level; contrast CT is the investigation of choice in adult small bowel obstruction; ultrasound is chosen for a child with intussusception. Write the ladder from memory.

You stored the imaging signs as one flat list. Each belongs to a disease and a test: coffee bean on plain film, bird's beak on enema, claw on enema, target and pseudokidney on ultrasound. Build a sign, disease, modality card.

You treated valvulae conniventes and haustra as one group of folds. Valvulae conniventes cross the full width and mark small bowel; haustra do not and mark large bowel. Sketch the two bowels with their folds.
You held 3, 6 and 9 as a rote string and shuffled the segments. Small bowel 3, colon 6, caecum 9, widening as you go distal. The widest segment perforates first. Redo the numbers card.
You read 'most' as one scale, so the commonest groin hernia became the riskiest. Strangulation risk follows a narrow rigid neck, so femoral leads. Pair each superlative with its exact qualifier.

You assumed strangulation always means complete obstruction and blurred the eponyms. Richter traps part of the wall and can strangulate without obstructing; Littre contains Meckel's diverticulum; Maydl has a W-shaped loop. Make a three-row eponym card.

You memorised the feature grid without the logic and reversed it. Bowel below a small bowel block still empties, so constipation is late; a large bowel block leaves little distal bowel, so constipation is early. High block vomits early. Re-derive it on paper.

You assumed a blocked gut is silent. In mechanical obstruction peristalsis fights a fixed block, so sounds are hyperactive and high-pitched; silence suggests paralytic ileus or late peritonitis. Reread the working-versus-failed gut contrast.

You used one rule, detorse, for every volvulus. Viable sigmoid: scope and flatus tube, then elective colectomy. Gangrene or perforation: Hartmann's. Caecal volvulus: right hemicolectomy. Order the steps: viability, site, then definitive operation.

You treated colicky pain as a fixed label for simple obstruction and missed the change. Constant severe pain with tachycardia, fever or localised guarding signals strangulation and needs theatre. Reread the strangulation card.

You applied the 72-hour trial to every obstruction. It applies only to adhesive obstruction without strangulation, hernia or closed loop; those go to theatre. Redo the override list: strangulation, obstructed hernia, closed loop, failed trial.

You treated 24, 24 to 48 and 72 hours as interchangeable. Contrast at 24 hours checks for resolution, a planned second look is at 24 to 48 hours, and 72 hours ends the non-operative trial. Draw one timeline.

You treated the operation as the first act and resuscitation as optional. Fluids with potassium, nasogastric decompression and a urinary catheter come first, as vomiting and third-space loss leave the patient dry. Say 'drip and suck first' before each management vignette.

You stretched a familiar large bowel condition to 'most common' and merged two caecal facts. Carcinoma is the commonest cause; sigmoid the commonest volvulus site; caecum the commonest perforation site. Keep the three separate.

You used one operation for every obstructing colon cancer. Name the side first: right gets hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis; left gets Hartmann's, or primary anastomosis in selected stable patients; a stent is a bridge or palliation for left-sided disease.

You sorted causes by name or organ rather than by wall relation. Gallstone is intraluminal; intussusception and strictures are intramural; adhesions, hernia and volvulus are extramural. Ask inside, in or outside for every cause.

You tend to skip the qualifier in the stem: surgical history, age, setting, side of the colon, or the pain change. Underline it before choosing, and ask what the answer would be on the other side of it.

You tend to get the order wrong, often reaching for theatre or a rule before the screen. Say the sequence aloud: resuscitate, check for strangulation, hernia and closed loop, then decide on trial or operation.

You tend to merge look-alikes: signs, folds and eponyms stored as one group. Fix it with side-by-side cards that name the single discriminating feature, such as folds crossing the lumen or not, or the test on which a sign is seen.
You tend to swap numbers. Attach each figure to a meaning, such as 3-6-9 to bowel calibre, or 24, 24 to 48 and 72 hours to the decision each governs, then retest them in application questions.

You tend to stretch a superlative beyond its qualifier. Commonest cause, commonest site, most likely to strangulate and most likely to perforate are different questions. Write the exact qualifier beside each answer.
You tend to reverse a mechanism: which end empties, or whether a blocked gut is loud or silent. Trace what happens above and below the block before filling any table.
Your confidence tracked your accuracy: Sure answers were right, and any Guessing answers mark what to review first. That is a useful revision signal, so trust it and start with the items you flagged.

You used no hints, even on the questions you missed. A hint after a first miss costs less than a second wrong answer and gives you a different angle on the stem. Use one the next time you are stuck, then compare what it changed.

Work through the cards in the order shown: confident errors first, then gaps, then shaky objectives. Review them at 1, 3, 7, 21 and 60 days. Redo the module in a week; the traps you fell into are the ones the exam is most likely to set again.
